claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 is in a hierarchical-heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
High-value microstructural descriptors can be obtained using relatively quick in-situ characterization techniques.
A reduced-order machine-learning model using those descriptors can rapidly predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
The reduced-order model will be comparably accurate to full-scale simulations.
Multiscale chemical fluctuations and phase distributions mediate the relationship between the microstructural inputs and macroscopic mechanical properties.
Selecting a limited set of high-information descriptors bypasses the need for computationally expensive full-scale simulations.
The selected descriptors capture the essential physics governing elastic, plastic, and fracture behavior.
Predictions of Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness will have approximately 5–10% error relative to experimental measurements.
The proposed approach will reduce computational demands by nearly an order of magnitude relative to traditional methods.
Prior thermophysical-parameter, CALPHAD, first-principles, and standard machine-learning approaches require large computational resources.
Prior approaches have limited predictive capability for fracture toughness.
The model will cease to be reliable when its descriptors do not capture the relevant heterogeneity.
Extreme disorder or unexpected phase transformations can place the system outside the model's reliable domain.
Failure of in-situ techniques to resolve critical microstructural features will make the method unreliable.
Accuracy and efficiency gains depend on the quality and representativeness of the selected descriptors.
Errors greater than 10% or a speed-up below 10× in a blinded prospective comparison would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome defines 5–10% as the absolute prediction error, whereas the uncertainty field calls the same range an 'accuracy improvement.' These are different quantities and cannot be treated interchangeably.
